elements.element: New York law governs the Agreement.
elements.evidence: Section 15.9 is left untouched and continues to provide that the Agreement "will be governed by the internal laws of the State of Delaware, USA". No New York choice-of-law language is proposed.

elements.element: State and federal courts in New York County have exclusive jurisdiction over the merits, subject only to temporary injunctive relief elsewhere.
elements.evidence: The inserted forum language in 15.10.1 reads "resolved exclusively by the state and federal courts located in the State of Delaware"; New York appears only as the seat for the now-optional ICDR arbitration in 15.10.2.2, not as a merits court forum.

elements.element: The governing law is Delaware, California, or England and Wales.
elements.evidence: Section 15.9 (unchanged): "will be governed by the internal laws of the State of Delaware, USA ... without regard to conflict of laws principles." Delaware is on the accepted fallback list, so no edit was required.

elements.element: The dispute forum is the corresponding Delaware or California courts, or the courts of London for England and Wales law.
elements.evidence: Amended 15.10.1: "such Dispute shall be resolved exclusively by the state and federal courts located in the State of Delaware, and each Party irrevocably submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of those courts." The mandatory ICDR submission is removed; 15.10.2.1 now permits arbitration "only if both Parties so agree in writing after the Dispute has arisen" and 15.10.2.2 applies only "[w]here the Parties have agreed in writing to arbitrate", so the ICDR competence-competence delegation over "scope or applicability" no longer overrides the court clause. Forum matches the Delaware governing law.

reasons: Fallback level is complete: Delaware law was already in place and is untouched, and the operative forum sentence now vests exclusive merits jurisdiction in the Delaware state and federal courts, matching the governing law.

The walk-away trigger (mandatory arbitration) is cured in operative language, not merely in the comment: both the submission clause (15.10.1) and the unilateral right to initiate (15.10.2.1) are converted to a bilateral written-agreement gate, and 15.10.2.2 (including the delegation of scope/applicability to the ICDR) is expressly conditioned on that gate, so no unqualified arbitration mandate survives to contradict the court clause.

Minimality holds: the three operations touch only the submission-to-forum words and the two arbitration-trigger lead-ins. Section 15.9, the executive escalation period, the Section 7.5.5 Material Impact route, the IP carve-out, the preliminary injunctive relief carve-out, the New York seat and the tribunal machinery are all retained verbatim, and the deletion of "including the determination of the scope or applicability of this agreement to arbitrate" is necessary to stop the tribunal from claiming jurisdiction over the new court clause.

Intent is preserved: the retained IP and Material Impact routes operate as express "[n]otwithstanding the foregoing" carve-outs from the new Delaware forum rather than as contradictory retained sentences, and the retained prohibition on arbitrating IP ownership/validity matters remains coherent under a consent-based arbitration regime. No undefined term or dangling cross-reference is created; "Dispute", "Executive Officers" and "ICDR" all remain defined and used.

Residual point to consider tightening (not an element failure at fallback): the retained IP carve-out sends ownership/validity merits disputes to "a U.S. federal court of appropriate jurisdiction", which is broader than Delaware. If we want a truly exclusive Delaware merits forum, that phrase should read "the U.S. federal court located in the State of Delaware"; as drafted the carve-out is a pre-existing, subject-matter-limited domestic route that does not restore arbitration or a foreign venue.

Also confirm downstream subsections of 15.10.2 (arbitrator selection, award, costs) contain no free-standing sentence assuming arbitration is mandatory; those paragraphs were not supplied, and any such sentence would need the same "[w]here the Parties have agreed in writing to arbitrate" gate to avoid inconsistency.
